name: Chapter 9: Biotechnology: Principles and Processes
description: Genetic engineering principles, restriction enzymes, gel electrophoresis, vectors, competent hosts, PCR, bioreactors and downstream processing

cards.term: Define biotechnology.
cards.definition: Techniques using live organisms or their enzymes to make products and processes useful to humans

cards.term: Biotechnology in the restricted modern sense?
cards.definition: Processes using genetically modified organisms on a large scale

cards.term: Other processes included in biotechnology?
cards.definition: IVF (test-tube baby), synthesising and using a gene, DNA vaccines, correcting a defective gene

cards.term: EFB definition of biotechnology?
cards.definition: "The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services"

cards.term: Who founded recombinant DNA technology (NCERT profile)?
cards.definition: Herbert Boyer (restriction enzymes, sticky ends) with Stanley Cohen (plasmids)

cards.term: Two core techniques of modern biotechnology?
cards.definition: Genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering

cards.term: What is genetic engineering?
cards.definition: Altering the chemistry of genetic material (DNA/RNA), introducing it into hosts to change the phenotype

cards.term: What is bioprocess engineering?
cards.definition:
Maintaining a sterile ambience so only the desired microbe/cell grows in large quantities.
Products: antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes

cards.term: Limitation of traditional hybridisation overcome by genetic engineering?
cards.definition: Hybridisation carries undesirable genes along; genetic engineering introduces only the desired gene(s)

cards.term: Why can’t an alien DNA piece multiply in a host on its own?
cards.definition: It needs an origin of replication; it must be part of a replicating chromosome or vector

cards.term: What is cloning?
cards.definition: Making multiple identical copies of a template DNA

cards.term: First recombinant DNA: who, when, what?
cards.definition: Cohen and Boyer, 1972: linked an antibiotic resistance gene to a native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium

cards.term: What is a plasmid?
cards.definition: Autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA

cards.term: Why is a plasmid called a vector?
cards.definition: Like a mosquito carries malaria, it delivers an alien piece of DNA into the host

cards.term: Enzyme joining antibiotic-resistance gene with plasmid?
cards.definition: DNA ligase

cards.term: What is recombinant DNA?
cards.definition: A new combination of circular, autonomously replicating DNA created in vitro

cards.term: Host used for cloning the first recombinant DNA?
cards.definition: Escherichia coli (related to Salmonella); used its own DNA polymerase

cards.term: Key tools of recombinant DNA technology?
cards.definition: Restriction enzymes, polymerases, ligases, vectors and the host organism

cards.term: When were restriction enzymes found, and why the name?
cards.definition: 1963: they restricted the growth of bacteriophage in E. coli

cards.term: Two enzymes isolated in 1963?
cards.definition: One added methyl groups to DNA; the other cut DNA (restriction endonuclease)

cards.term: First restriction endonuclease, and its recognition?
cards.definition: Hind II: cuts at a specific six base pair recognition sequence

cards.term: How many restriction enzymes are known?
cards.definition: More than 900, from over 230 bacterial strains

cards.term: Naming convention: EcoRI?
cards.definition: E = genus Escherichia, co = species coli, R = strain RY 13, I = order of isolation

cards.term: Exonuclease vs endonuclease?
cards.definition: Exonuclease: removes nucleotides from the ends. Endonuclease: cuts at specific positions within DNA.

cards.term: How does a restriction endonuclease work?
cards.definition: "Inspects" DNA, binds its specific recognition sequence, cuts both strands in the sugar-phosphate backbone

cards.term: What is a DNA palindrome?
cards.definition: Sequence reading the same on both strands when read in the same orientation (5′→3′)

cards.term: EcoRI recognition sequence?
cards.definition: 5′-GAATTC-3′ / 3′-CTTAAG-5′

cards.term: What are sticky ends?
cards.definition:
Single-stranded overhangs left because the enzyme cuts a little away from the centre of the palindrome.
They H-bond with complementary ends

cards.term: What do sticky ends facilitate?
cards.definition: Action of DNA ligase

cards.term: Why must vector and source DNA be cut by the same enzyme?
cards.definition: To get the same kind of sticky ends that can be joined

cards.term: Create a palindrome from 5′-GGATCC-3′: is it one? (Exercise 7)
cards.definition: Yes: complement read 5′→3′ is also GGATCC (BamHI site)

cards.term: Do eukaryotic cells have restriction endonucleases? (Exercise 5)
cards.definition: No (typically); they are a bacterial defence against phages, bacterial DNA protected by methylation

cards.term: Why doesn’t a bacterium cut its own DNA? (intuition)
cards.definition: Its own recognition sites are methylated by the partner methylase enzyme

cards.term: Separation technique for DNA fragments?
cards.definition: Gel electrophoresis

cards.term: Why does DNA move towards the anode?
cards.definition: DNA is negatively charged

cards.term: Matrix used in electrophoresis?
cards.definition: Agarose, a natural polymer from sea weeds

cards.term: How are fragments separated in agarose?
cards.definition: By size through a sieving effect; smaller fragments move farther

cards.term: How is DNA visualised in the gel?
cards.definition: Stain with ethidium bromide, expose to UV → bright orange bands

cards.term: Read Figure 9.3: where was the sample loaded?
cards.definition: At the wells (top); largest fragments near wells, smallest farthest

cards.term: What is elution?
cards.definition: Cutting out DNA bands from the gel and extracting the DNA

cards.term: Why are plasmids and phages useful vectors?
cards.definition: They replicate independently of chromosomal DNA phages have very high copy number plasmids 1–2 to 15–100 copies

cards.text: Features required in a cloning vector: {{c1::origin of replication (ori)}}, {{c2::selectable marker}}, {{c3::cloning sites}}, and for plants/animals, suitable {{c4::vectors}}.

cards.term: Role of ori?
cards.definition: Where replication starts; also controls copy number of linked DNA

cards.term: What is a selectable marker?
cards.definition: Helps identify and eliminate non-transformants and permit transformants to grow

cards.term: Common selectable markers for E. coli?
cards.definition: Resistance to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, kanamycin

cards.term: What is transformation?
cards.definition: Introducing a piece of DNA into a host bacterium

cards.term: Why should a vector have few (preferably one) recognition sites?
cards.definition: Multiple sites generate several fragments, complicating cloning

cards.term: Figure 9.4 · pBR322
What does rop code for in pBR322?
cards.definition: Proteins involved in replication of the plasmid

cards.term: Antibiotic resistance genes in pBR322?
cards.definition: ampᴿ and tetᴿ

cards.term: Insertion at BamH I in pBR322: selection?
cards.definition:
Recombinants lose tetracycline resistance but keep ampicillin:
they grow on ampicillin, not on tetracycline
Non-recombinants grow on both

cards.term: What is insertional inactivation?
cards.definition: Inserting DNA within a gene (e.g. β-galactosidase) inactivates it

cards.term: Blue-white selection?
cards.definition: With a chromogenic substrate: blue = no insert (β-gal active). Colourless (white) = recombinant.

cards.term: Why is blue-white better than antibiotic inactivation?
cards.definition: Antibiotic method needs simultaneous plating on two plates; blue-white needs one

cards.term: How can a reporter enzyme monitor transformation? (Exercise 9)
cards.definition: Its visible activity (e.g. colour from β-galactosidase) shows which cells took up and express the foreign DNA

cards.term: Plant vector derived from a pathogen?
cards.definition: Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens, disarmed to deliver genes without causing tumours

cards.term: What does wild Agrobacterium do?
cards.definition: Delivers T-DNA that transforms dicot plant cells into a tumour making chemicals for the pathogen

cards.term: Animal vectors derived from pathogens?
cards.definition: Disarmed retroviruses (which normally make cells cancerous)

cards.term: Correction: NCERT spells "Agrobacterium tumifaciens". Correct?
cards.definition: Agrobacterium tumefaciens

cards.term: Why can’t DNA pass through cell membranes?
cards.definition: DNA is hydrophilic

cards.term: How are bacteria made competent?
cards.definition: Treat with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium

cards.term: Heat-shock method?
cards.definition: Incubate cells with rDNA on ice → briefly at 42 °C → back on ice

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints "420C" for heat shock. Correct?
cards.definition: 42 °C

cards.term: Methods of introducing DNA into hosts
cards.definition: Micro-injection: rDNA injected directly into nucleus of animal cell; Biolistics (gene gun): Plant cells bombarded with gold/tungsten particles coated with DNA; Disarmed pathogen vectors: Infect the cell and transfer rDNA; Heat shock (Ca²⁺): Competent bacteria take up plasmid

cards.text: Steps of rDNA technology: isolation of DNA → {{c1::fragmentation by restriction endonucleases}} → isolation of desired fragment → {{c2::ligation into a vector}} → {{c3::transfer into host}} → culturing at large scale → {{c4::extraction of product}}.

cards.term: Why must DNA be pure before cutting?
cards.definition: Restriction enzymes need DNA free from other macromolecules

cards.term: Enzymes to release DNA
cards.definition: Bacteria: Lysozyme; Plant cells: Cellulase; Fungus: Chitinase

cards.term: How are RNA and proteins removed?
cards.definition: RNA by ribonuclease; proteins by protease

cards.term: How is purified DNA finally precipitated?
cards.definition: By adding chilled ethanol; seen as fine threads removed by spooling

cards.term: What is chitinase? (Exercise 11c)
cards.definition: Enzyme that breaks chitin of fungal cell walls to release DNA

cards.term: How is progress of restriction digestion checked?
cards.definition: Agarose gel electrophoresis

cards.term: How is recombinant DNA prepared after cutting?
cards.definition: Mix cut gene of interest with cut vector and add ligase

cards.term: What does PCR stand for?
cards.definition: Polymerase Chain Reaction

cards.term: What are primers?
cards.definition: Small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of DNA

cards.text: Each PCR cycle: {{c1::denaturation}} (heat) → {{c2::annealing}} of primers → {{c3::extension}} by DNA polymerase.

cards.term: Figure 9.6 · PCR
Thermostable polymerase in PCR and source?
cards.definition: Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus

cards.term: Why is a thermostable polymerase essential?
cards.definition: It stays active during the high-temperature denaturation step, so it needn’t be re-added each cycle

cards.term: Amplification by PCR?
cards.definition: About 1 billion copies (≈ 30 cycles, since\[2^{30} \approx 10^9\])

cards.term: Why does 30 cycles give ~a billion copies? (intuition)
cards.definition: Copies double every cycle: \( 2^{10} \approx 1000 \), so \( 2^{30} \approx 1000^3 = 10^9 \)

cards.term: How are transformants selected with an ampicillin marker?
cards.definition: Spread on ampicillin plates: only transformants grow; untransformed cells die

cards.term: What is a recombinant protein?
cards.definition: Protein from a gene expressed in a heterologous host

cards.term: What is a continuous culture system?
cards.definition:
Used medium is drained from one side, fresh medium added from the other.
Cells are kept in log/exponential phase → more biomass and yield

cards.term: What are bioreactors?
cards.definition:
Vessels where raw materials are biologically converted into products using microbial, plant, animal or human cells.
Volume 100–1000 L

cards.term: Optimum conditions provided by a bioreactor?
cards.definition: Temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen

cards.term: Most common bioreactors?
cards.definition: Stirred-tank type: cylindrical or curved base for mixing

cards.term: Components of a stirred-tank bioreactor?
cards.definition: Agitator, oxygen delivery, foam control, temperature control, pH control, sampling ports

cards.term: Simple vs sparged stirred-tank bioreactor?
cards.definition: Sparged: sterile air bubbles increase the oxygen transfer area

cards.term: Advantages of stirred tank over shake flask (Exercise 6)?
cards.definition: Large volumes, controlled temperature, pH, foam, sampling, continuous culture and sterile operation

cards.term: What is downstream processing?
cards.definition: Separation and purification of the product after biosynthesis

cards.term: Steps after purification before marketing?
cards.definition: Formulation with preservatives, clinical trials (for drugs) and strict quality control

cards.term: Tools of genetic engineering
cards.definition: Restriction endonuclease: Molecular scissors; DNA ligase: Molecular glue; Plasmid / phage: Vector (vehicle); Taq polymerase: Amplifies DNA in PCR; Agarose gel: Separates DNA by size; Ethidium bromide + UV: Visualises DNA
